c1.label: Q1
c1.prompt: What does the accelerometer on the remote measure?

C.text: How fast the car is going

D.text: How far the remote is from the car

c1.why: It reports the pull of gravity along each axis, which is how a board knows which way it is leaning.

c2.label: Q2
c2.prompt: The tilt reading runs to about 1024, but wheel speed stops at 100. What has to happen?

B.text: The number has to be scaled down before it is used

C.text: The remote must be tilted less

D.text: The radio converts it for you

c2.why: Dividing brings the range down to something the motors can actually use. Without it, almost every tilt is full speed.

c3.label: Q3
c3.prompt: `send value "x" 40` sends two things. What are they?
c3.why: The name is what lets one program send more than one kind of number — the receiver sorts them by name.

r1.label: Q1
r1.prompt: A message arrives with name "y" and value 30. What changes?
r1.why: Only the branch whose name matches runs. That is what the name is for.

r2.label: Q2
r2.prompt: `xValue` is 0 and `yValue` is 50. What do the wheels do?
r2.why: With no side tilt the two sums are equal, and equal wheels are a straight line.

r3.label: Q3
r3.prompt: `xValue` is 20 and `yValue` is 0. What does the car do?
r3.why: The wheels come out at 20 and -20 — opposite directions, same size. That is a turn in place.

r4.label: Q4
r4.prompt: This is on the remote. What is wrong with the number it sends?

A.text: It is far too large for a wheel speed

C.text: It goes to the wrong radio group

r4.why: Raw tilt runs to about 1024. Sent straight through, almost any lean asks for far more speed than a wheel has.

d1.label: Q1
d1.prompt: The car slams to full speed at the tiniest tilt. Which change fixes it?

D.text: Divide each reading by 10 before sending

d1.why: Scaling is the missing step. Dividing brings a 1024-range number into the range the wheels can use.

d2.label: Q2
d2.prompt: The car turns but never drives forward or back. What is missing?

A.text: The branch that stores the "y" value

d2.why: `yValue` stays at 0 forever, so the wheels only ever get `+x` and `-x` — opposite speeds, which is a turn.

b1.label: Q1
b1.prompt: Put the remote's loop in order: 1 send both values · 2 read the tilt on both axes · 3 divide each reading down
b1.why: Measure, scale, send. Sending before scaling puts the raw number on the air.

b2.label: Q2
b2.prompt: On the car, where does the motor block belong?

A.text: On the remote, after the sends

B.text: Nowhere — the radio value drives the wheels by itself

C.text: In a `forever` loop of its own

b2.why: The handler's job is to store the newest numbers. A loop then drives from whatever is stored, whether or not a message just arrived.
